Hi marques I’m thinking about upgrading my iPhone 12 Pro, do you recommend the 17 pro?

If you take my advice, do not buy the iPhone 17 Pro. I purchased it three months ago, and now the front speaker isn't working. The battery life is also terrible; it drains on its own even when the phone isn't being used. It is an absolutely worthless phone.

What I’m finding really frustrating is the power buttons placement. It’s literally directly under my thumb when I’m holding the phone during a call. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve cut off a call just by accidentally holding the phone ‘too hard’. Anyone else experiencing this?

This is more or less why I ended up going for the iPhone 17 Pro Max.

I was actually looking hard at the Android Ultra phones first, especially Oppo and Xiaomi, because on paper they are closer to the kind of camera phone I wanted. Bigger sensors, more zoom, more camera-style controls, and in some cases 6000 mAh batteries and faster charging. For photography, especially when I do not want to walk around with my Nikon D7500 hanging around my neck, that kind of phone makes sense.

Problem is, the phones I wanted were not really practical for me. Oppo was not available through 3 where I normally have my phone stuff, and the Xiaomi was not something I could get on the kind of payment plan that made sense for me. I could get an iPhone or Samsung much easier in Denmark, with normal warranty and no import/marketplace headache. 3 also would not approve the phone plan for some weird reason, even though I have been a customer for years and paid off my iPhone 13 Pro fine, so I ended up doing it through Elgiganten instead.

I also use both Android and iPhone already, so I am not one of those “only Apple” people. My Android is a Ulefone Armor X31 Pro. I use that mostly for media, MitID/bank, Maps and battery life. It is rugged and practical, but the camera is not great. Low light is weak, no proper stabilization like a real camera phone, and Google Camera ports can only do so much when the hardware is not there.

My iPhone 13 Pro is still my main phone for calls/eSIM and the better camera. I have had it for around 3 years and 10 months, and honestly it has held up well. A few screen scratches from ending up in the same pocket as keys, some small marks on the metal edge and back, but nothing crazy. It is still working. That is also why I do not mind going Pro Max again, because I actually keep phones for years, not 6 months.

For me the 17 Pro Max makes sense because it is not chasing thinness. I do not care about a super thin phone if it means worse battery, worse cooling or less camera hardware. Make it thicker, give it more battery, better thermals, better cameras and USB-C. That is far more useful to me than having the thinnest phone in the room.

The Android Ultra phones may still win in some areas on paper, especially crazy zoom, battery size and charging speed. But the iPhone 17 Pro Max is the safer full package for my use: main phone, camera phone, good video, Live Photos, long software support, normal Danish purchase, and it fits into how I already use my phones.

It will not replace my Nikon for real wildlife or zoo photography, but for places like BonBon-Land, Experimentarium, bunkers, travel days, shops, food, random details and places where a DSLR just feels stupid to carry around, it should be a huge upgrade from my 13 Pro.

Why don’t tech reviewers talk about privacy when reviewing new devices?

Most reviews focus on things like camera quality, performance, battery life, and new features. That’s great, but shouldn’t privacy also be an important part of the review? Many tech companies showcase impressive innovations during launches, but users rarely hear about how much data these devices collect or how that data could potentially be used.

Over the years we’ve seen whistleblowers and discussions about mass data collection, and many people already live with the feeling that large amounts of personal data are constantly being gathered. If that’s the case, shouldn’t reviewers also research and explain the privacy side of the technology they are promoting?

There have also been reports about surveillance tools like Pegasus that can exploit vulnerabilities in smartphones and gain access to sensitive information. Situations like this show that even devices from major companies can sometimes be vulnerable, and users rarely hear about these risks during normal tech reviews.

It would be really valuable for viewers to know not only whether a device is fast or has a good camera, but also whether it respects user privacy, how secure it actually is, and what kind of data it collects. Technology reviewers have huge audiences, so including privacy and security analysis could help people make more informed decisions about the devices they use every day.
